claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin native oxide layer.
The native oxide layer is a mixture of iron oxides on a ferrite-pearlite microstructure.
Elevated-temperature exposure in a harsh environment accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel relative to room-temperature exposure.
Thermal stresses induce microcracking of the native oxide film.
A mismatch in thermal expansion between the steel substrate and its native oxide causes stress to build up at elevated temperatures.
Microcracking compromises the protective function of the native oxide film.
Cracks in the native oxide expose fresh underlying steel to the electrolyte.
Exposure of fresh steel through oxide cracks to chloride-containing electrolyte enhances localized galvanic corrosion.
An intact native oxide film suppresses corrosion-related degradation.
Thermal cycling around 70 degrees Celsius will produce more oxide-film microcracks than room-temperature exposure.
Elevated-temperature thermal cycling will increase corrosion current density relative to the room-temperature reference.
Elevated-temperature thermal cycling will decrease polarization resistance relative to the room-temperature reference.
Pits will be more prevalent after elevated-temperature thermal cycling than after room-temperature exposure.
Room-temperature Q235 samples in 3.5 wt% NaCl will retain a relatively intact native oxide and have lower corrosion rates.
The proposed microcracking mechanism is expected to be dominant for steel bearing an unmodified native oxide layer.
Pre-passivation, chloride concentration, temperature, oxide composition, microstructure, impurities, and alloying variations may alter oxide stability or the applicability of the mechanism.
